name: Sloop 28

places.name: Cockpit
places.description: You're in the cockpit, teak-slatted seats worn pale, the tiller beside you and the key panel on the bulkhead.

places.name: Companionway
places.description: You're in the companionway hatch, a hand on the cold grab rail, the saloon below and the quarter berth at your knee.

places.name: Quarter berth
places.description: You're in the quarter berth, knees on the cushion, the engine panel by your shoulder.

places.name: Saloon
places.description: You're in the saloon, the table folded, the air cool and a little damp.

places.name: Forepeak
places.description: You're in the forepeak, bent under the deck hatch, sail bags and a coil of old anchor warp around your feet.

places.name: On deck
places.description: You're up on deck, the mast stepped in the middle, dew on the cabin top and the whole yard laid out below.

places.name: Beside the hull
places.description: You're on the gravel beside the hull, her keel at head height and the cradle pads around you.
places.way: down the ladder to the ground beside the hull

covers.name: Companionway steps
covers.removeText: You lift the steps out and stand them against the bulkhead; the front of the engine looks up at you.
covers.refitText: You slot the steps back into their runners and they sit square.

covers.name: Quarter-berth panel
covers.removeText: Two screws, a tug on the plywood, and the side of the engine is open to you.
covers.refitText: You hold the panel up to its frame and run the two screws home.

covers.name: Battery-box lid
covers.removeText: You unhook the lid and fold it back on its pin; the smell of acid comes up with the cold.
covers.refitText: You fold the lid down and hook it shut.

covers.name: Cockpit-locker lid
covers.removeText: You lift the seat lid and prop it open; fenders, a tin of rags, and the tank down below.
covers.refitText: You lower the seat lid and sit on it to be sure.

covers.name: Saloon floorboards
covers.removeText: You lift the floorboards one by one and stack them on the settee; the bilge smells of brine.
covers.refitText: You lay the floorboards back in their order, shoulder to shoulder.

covers.name: Companionway hatch
covers.refitText: You slide the hatch shut and drop in the washboard.

covers.name: Bilge pump fuse
covers.removeText: You pull the bilge pump fuse out of its holder.
covers.refitText: You push the bilge pump fuse back into its holder.
covers.refitLog: Put the bilge pump fuse back in.

positions.label: Below the companionway, above the engine

components.name: Start battery
components.description: A black 70 Ah lead-acid battery, case dusty, date stamped three summers back. The vents are dry.

faults.name: Battery at 60 % charge

reveals.text: Resting voltage says about 60 %.

faults.consequence: Slow cranking, and a flat battery after a few starts.

yard.how: The yard fits a new battery

faults.name: Battery soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: A tide line of bilge scum on the battery case, the terminals furred green underneath.

faults.consequence: The battery leaks its charge away and will not hold it for long.

yard.how: The yard fits a new battery

components.name: Battery switch
components.description: A red-knobbed rotary switch, knob faded pink where the light from the hatch falls on it. It turns with a gritty click.

components.name: Positive terminal
components.description: A lead clamp under a red rubber boot, bolt snug.

removablePart.name: rubber boot
removablePart.uncoveredText: Under the boot the lead is clean and bright.

faults.name: Strained positive terminal

reveals.text: The clamp is discoloured with heat, bluish at the edge, and the lug is bent from the long drags on the starter.
The meter shows a real drop across the clamp while she cranks: it is eating volts.

faults.consequence: The starter gets less and less each time; one day it only clicks.

diy.how: Clean the clamp and straighten the lug, or fit a new terminal

yard.how: The yard fits a new terminal and lug

components.name: Main positive cable
components.description: A fat red cable, sleeve stiff with age but unbroken. It runs forward along the box wall.

components.name: Negative terminal
components.description: A lead clamp under a black rubber boot, greasy from some earlier owner's smear of vaseline.

faults.name: Corroded negative terminal

reveals.text: The lead under the boot is crusted green-white, the crust eating into the clamp.
That's far too much voltage lost across one clamp.
You pull the clamp off and find a ring of green-white crust on the post, eating into the lead.

faults.consequence: The engine won't start.

diy.how: Clean the post and clamp, and tighten it

yard.how: The yard electrician cleans and re-terminates the battery cables

components.name: Negative cable
components.description: A black cable of the same gauge as its red twin, a little greener at the lugs.

components.name: Engine ground stud
components.description: A brass stud on the engine foot with a ring lug and a nut. Dull, but it holds.

faults.name: Engine ground stud soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: The ground stud wears a crust of bilge scum, the ring lug green and the nut rusted fast.

faults.consequence: The ground connection resists the starter's current and the engine cranks slowly.

diy.how: Clean and tighten the stud, or fit a new one

yard.how: The yard cleans the ground stud

components.name: Starter solenoid
components.description: A small silver can bolted on top of the starter. Paint blistered; it clicks when called.

components.name: Starter motor
components.description: A heavy cylinder on the flywheel housing, caked with old oil and a fine grey dust. Smells of warm copper.
components.note: seriesOhms 0.045 is an unverified placeholder, decision 2

faults.name: Starter soaked in bilge water

reveals.text: A tide line of bilge scum on the starter body, rust blooming at the bolts.

faults.consequence: The starter cranks slower as the corrosion works in, and one day it will not turn.

yard.how: The yard fits a new starter motor

components.name: Ignition panel
components.description: A cockpit panel with a key, two warning lamps and a tachometer that has read 800 for years. The plastic has clouded.

components.name: Fuel tank
components.description: A grey aluminium tank under the cockpit sole, tidy welds, a little white bloom at the bottom seam.

faults.name: Water in the fuel tank

reveals.text: Under the diesel a clear line of water sits in the bottom of the bowl, two fingers deep, a wobbling skin where they meet. You drain it off into a jar.

faults.consequence: In a seaway the water is stirred up into the filter: the engine fires and dies when you need it.
faults.laterNote: a tow if she stops in the wrong place

diy.how: Drain the filter bowl on three separate days, then fit a new primary filter element

yard.how: The yard drains and polishes the tank and changes the filters

components.name: Fuel shutoff valve
components.description: A brass lever valve on the tank outlet. The lever is stiff but moves the full quarter turn.

components.name: Fuel supply line
components.description: A clear-sleeved fuel hose, slightly yellowed, clamped at both ends. No weeping at the clamps.

components.name: Primary fuel filter / water separator
components.description: A spin-on filter with a glass bowl below. The element is dusty; a date is faintly visible on the casing.

faults.name: Primary fuel filter half clogged

reveals.text: You open the drain and look in the bowl: dark diesel, and black sludge clinging to the walls.
An old date is written on the element in marker, so old that the ink has gone brown.

faults.consequence: Fuel starvation when the sea stirs the tank up: she runs rough or stops.

yard.how: The yard changes the fuel filters

components.name: Lift pump
components.description: A small pump on the front of the block with a priming lever. Ticks when the engine turns.

components.name: Secondary fuel filter
components.description: A small blue-grey canister on the front of the engine, clean on the outside, with a single ring of rust at the base.

components.name: Injection pump
components.description: A compact pump with a stamped plate, bolted tight. The tamper seals are intact.

components.name: Injectors
components.description: Two stubby injectors under their return pipes, a little carbon around the clamps.

components.name: Fuel return line
components.description: A thin hose back to the tank, clamped with a worm-drive that has started to rust.

components.name: Raw-water seacock
components.description: A bronze ball valve on a through-hull, green with age, the handle stiff.
components.replaceText: You knock out the old seacock, bed a new through-hull and ball valve, and double-clamp the hose.

faults.name: Weeping raw-water seacock

reveals.text: There's a damp patch in the bilge under the seacock, rimmed with white salt crust.
Salt crust round the valve stem and a bead of water hanging under it: the seacock is weeping at the stem.

escalation.text: The raw-water seacock has seized: the salt has crusted the stem solid and the handle won't move.

faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 6): seizing is driven by frost; rain counts only with the saloon floorboards up. Weep rate 0.05 L/h is also unverified (decision 1).
faults.consequence: It weeps now and will seize; a seized seacock can't be shut if a hose lets go.

yard.how: The yard replaces the seacock and through-hull

faults.name: Seized raw-water seacock

reveals.text: You lean on the seacock handle. It doesn't move at all: seized solid in the salt.

faults.consequence: Seized shut: no cooling water, the engine overheats within minutes.

diy.how: Cut out and replace the seacock and through-hull

yard.how: The yard cuts out and replaces the seacock

components.name: Raw-water strainer
components.description: A clear-lidded strainer, a little weed and grit in the basket and a faint tidemark inside the glass.

components.name: Raw-water pump
components.description: A bronze-bodied pump on the front of the engine, a faint salt trail beneath the shaft seal.

components.name: Raw-water impeller
components.description: A rubber impeller, inside the pump behind a six-screw cover.

faults.name: Tired impeller

reveals.text: With the pump cover off, the vanes have taken a set in a curve and two of them are cracked at the root.
The water at the exhaust comes in weaker spurts than you would like.

faults.consequence: The engine will overheat under load at sea: you'll lose cooling when you need it most.
faults.laterNote: a tow home if it sheds its vanes

yard.how: The yard mechanic fits a new impeller

removablePart.name: raw-water pump cover
removablePart.uncoverText: You undo the six screws and lift off the raw-water pump cover.
removablePart.refitText: You put the pump cover back with a new gasket and do up the six screws.

components.name: Heat exchanger
components.description: A cylindrical exchanger with end caps, a thin white crust along one seam, no drips.

components.name: Thermostat
components.description: Hidden in its housing, as it should be. The housing gasket is dry and a little brittle.

components.name: Coolant
components.description: Green-pink coolant in the header tank, a shade murkier than it was. Level at the line.

components.name: Exhaust elbow
components.description: A cast elbow where the water meets the exhaust, a rust-brown stain at the lower flange.

components.name: Exhaust hose
components.description: A black wet-exhaust hose looping up under the cockpit, stiff, not cracked, clamps doubled.

faults.name: Exhaust hose cooked

reveals.text: The hose by the elbow is hard and blistered, the rubber cooked brown: it ran hot and dry.

faults.consequence: It will split and pour exhaust and water into the boat when she runs.

diy.how: Fit a new wet-exhaust hose and clamps

yard.how: The yard fits a new exhaust hose

components.name: Anti-siphon loop
components.description: A vented loop high in the cockpit locker, with a little white salt around the vent.

components.name: Engine block
components.description: A grey Nordvik twin-cylinder, paint worn at the corners, a faint sheen of oil beneath the sump.

components.name: Engine oil
components.description: The dipstick shows oil the colour of tea, within the marks.

components.name: Oil filter
components.description: A blue spin-on canister, rust around the base, a last service sticker curling at the edge.

components.name: Alternator
components.description: A small 60 A alternator on the front bracket, grimy but turning freely by hand.

components.name: Alternator belt
components.description: A narrow V-belt with a glazed shine on the flanks and a small dusting of black on the pulley.

faults.name: Slipping alternator belt

reveals.text: You press the belt mid-span: it gives a good inch, and the flanks are glazed. It's slipping on the pulley.

faults.consequence: The battery isn't charging while she runs; it will go flat.

diy.how: Fit a new belt and set the tension

yard.how: The yard fits a new belt

components.name: Glow plugs
components.description: Two glow plugs sunk into the head, thin wires on their caps, a fleck of carbon at each.
components.note: healthyOhms 0.8 is an unverified placeholder, decision 4

components.name: Hull
components.description: Cream gelcoat gone chalky, a few spider cracks at the toerail and a faded waterline stripe.

faults.name: Blistered old paint at the bow

reveals.text: You press a blister at the bow with a thumbnail. It is old paint lifting off older paint, dry and hollow; the gelcoat underneath is hard and sound. Not osmosis.

faults.consequence: Nothing: old paint lifting, the laminate is sound.

components.name: Keel
components.description: A cast-iron keel, rust bleeding from the bolts at the joint, a thin line of filler along the seam.

components.name: Rudder
components.description: A spade rudder with a small bit of play at the bottom, the blade fair and sound.

components.name: Standing rig
components.description: A tall alloy mast, shrouds a little dull, turnbuckles safety-wired in tape that has seen better summers.

components.name: Antifouling
components.description: Red-brown bottom paint, chalky and thin at the waterline, with a few patches of old blue beneath.
components.replaceText: You sand, wipe down and roll on two fresh coats of antifouling.

faults.name: Thin antifouling

reveals.text: The paint is worn through to the old primer along the waterline and on the leading edge of the keel.

faults.consequence: Weed and barnacles by midsummer: a knot slower, and a scrub that needs a lift.
faults.laterNote: afloat: needs a lift and a scrub

diy.how: Sand and roll on two coats of antifouling

yard.how: The yard paints the bottom

components.name: Navigation lights
components.description: A bicolour light on the pulpit and a white stern light, the wiring taped where it runs down the stanchion.
components.replaceText: You fit a new lens on the bicolour light and seal the gasket.

faults.name: Cracked navigation light lens

reveals.text: The bicolour lens has a crack through the red side, and there's a bead of water inside.

faults.consequence: Water gets into the fitting and the bow light fails at night.

yard.how: The yard electrician fits a new lens

components.name: Cockpit drain hoses
components.description: Two reinforced hoses from the cockpit drains down to their through-hulls, each held by a pair of hose clamps.
components.replaceText: You fit new stainless hose clamps, two to each hose tail.

faults.name: Rusted cockpit drain hose clamps
faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 1): 1.5 L of rain in per mm through the rusted clamps.

reveals.text: The clamps are rusted through at the screw housing; one crumbles when you press it with a thumb.

escalation.text: The cockpit drain hose has come off its tail: a rusted clamp let go and the hose slipped off the through-hull.

faults.consequence: A clamp that lets go floods the boat through the drain through-hull.
faults.laterNote: can be done afloat, with the drain seacock shut

yard.how: The yard renews the clamps

faults.name: Cockpit drain hose off its tail
faults.note: UNVERIFIED (decision 1): 60 L/h afloat through the open through-hull.

arrivalSign.text: The cockpit drain hose hangs loose from its tail; you can see it through the gap at the cockpit-locker lid. Worth lifting the lid.

reveals.text: The drain hose has slipped right off its through-hull tail and hangs loose; the rusted clamps lie in the bottom of the locker.

faults.consequence: With the hose off, the through-hull is open to the sea and the cockpit no longer drains.
faults.laterNote: can be done afloat, with the drain seacock shut

diy.how: Push the hose back on its tail and fit new doubled clamps

yard.how: The yard refits the drain hose with new clamps

components.name: Lifelines
components.description: Plastic-coated wire lifelines on four stanchions each side, swaged terminals at the pulpit and pushpit.
components.replaceText: You fit new lifeline terminals and tension the wires.

faults.name: Pitted lifeline terminals

reveals.text: Under the plastic the swaged terminals at the pushpit are pitted, rust weeping where the wire goes in.

faults.consequence: A terminal that lets go when someone falls against it.

yard.how: The yard rigger renews the terminals

components.name: Bilge
components.description: The lowest part of the hull under the saloon sole, where everything that gets in ends up.

components.name: Bilge pump
components.description: A small submersible pump bolted down at the lowest point of the bilge, a float switch on a short arm beside it. A two-core cable runs aft and up to the battery, through a fuse in a holder by the battery switch.
components.replaceText: You unbolt the old pump, bolt a new one down at the low point, fit the float switch beside it and splice the cable.

faults.name: Burnt-out bilge pump

reveals.text: The pump body is hot-smelling and the impeller housing is scorched; it hums but nothing moves.

faults.consequence: The bilge has no pump: whatever comes in stays in, and the float switch clicks for nothing.

diy.how: Fit a new pump and float switch

yard.how: The yard fits a new bilge pump

opening: As instructed I surveyed your 28-foot sloop ashore in her cradle at the yard. The hull was sounded and viewed from the ground, the deck and rig from deck level, the machinery as found. The engine was tried. I did not go aloft or strip any machinery.
My findings, in the order I made them:
closing: Items marked Before launch should be attended to before she goes in. The rest can be planned over the season.

items.text: Blistering noted at the bow below the waterline, possibly osmotic. Recommend moisture readings and a closer inspection.
Thin, worn to primer at the waterline and on the keel's leading edge. Recommend a fresh coat before launch.
Weeping at the stem, with salt crust in the bilge below. Recommend service or replacement before launch.
Hose clamps rusted, one failing. Recommend renewal, doubled.
Terminals pitted, rust weeping at the swages aft. Recommend replacement.
Bicolour lens cracked, water inside. Recommend replacement.
No defects visible from deck level. A rigger's inspection aloft is recommended within two seasons.
Dated three seasons back, history unknown. Recommend a load test, and replacement if it does not hold up.
On a trial start the starter clicked once and did not turn the engine. Poor cranking; recommend investigation of the starter circuit.
A sample drawn from the bottom of the tank shows free water. Recommend draining and polishing the tank, and new filters, before launch.
Element marked with a date well past its service interval. Recommend a new element.
Light external rust at the flange, no weeping. Serviceable; monitor.

electrical.name: Connection not done up tight (your own work)
electrical.reveal: Looking again at your own work, the connection moves when you wiggle it: not done up tight.
electrical.consequence: It can work loose under way and leave you without power.

diy.how: Redo it and tighten it properly

yard.how: The yard electrician redoes it

cooling.name: Hose clamp not seated (your own work)
cooling.reveal: A bead of water hangs under the hose clamp you fitted: it isn't seated square.
cooling.consequence: A slow weep that grows into a leak under way.

yard.how: The yard redoes the job

fuel.name: Fuel union not tightened (your own work)
fuel.reveal: A smell of diesel, and a wet ring round the union you did up.
fuel.consequence: Air gets in under way and the engine stops.

yard.how: The yard mechanic redoes it

engine.name: Part not seated right (your own work)
engine.reveal: What you fitted isn't sitting right: it shifts when you push it.
engine.consequence: It works loose with the vibration under way.

yard.how: The yard mechanic redoes it

hull.name: Patchy work (your own)
hull.reveal: Your work has thin patches and a run or two.

yard.how: The yard redoes it

water.soleText: Water stands over the saloon sole.
